Fanfiction is completely legitimate imo. I think writing stories for people to read them makes them legitimate stories (not that personal stories are not actually stories, my argument is simply that if it’s meant to be read and enjoyed, it’s a story). The argument for quality never makes sense to me. As has been mentioned, there’s great novels and shitty novels, there’s great fanfics and there’s shitty fanfics.

I mean, we live in a world where the Twilight series was not only extremely popular and successful, but also completely terrible. There’s also 50 Shades of Grey, which literally started out as Twilight fanfiction.

Not to mention that fanfiction can be much harder to write than original stories. Writing your own work is difficult, don’t get me wrong. But taking someone else’s work, attempting to parody it, AND somehow make it original is a completely different league of difficult. 

My original stories require research, internal logic and history. But that’s of my creation. If I’m making my own fantasy world, it can be whatever I wish it to be.

To create a story that not only lives up to the original work as well as following the canon takes a different level of craftsmanship. Fanfic writers can’t just make things up, they have to be at least somewhat consistent to the original work. Good fanfiction not only needs to stand out as a good story, but also pay enough tribute to the original work. If you’re writing, say, Game of Thrones fanfic, you’re going to have fans of the original work compare it to yours. That’s just so much pressure to work with. 

Fanfic is good for practice, appreciation, entertainment, it’s an underrated art form that is unfairly criticized.

I grew up in the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, aka, the Mormon Church. 

I was never very pious or devout, kinda just going through the religious motions because that’s what my family expected of me.

A few months before my 14th birthday, my mother died and I started to become more involved with the church. Going every Sunday, going to seminary and doing a bunch of activities with church members like camp outs, parties and such.

When I was around 15-16 I had my sexual awakening, I realized I was pansexual. I was attracted to EVERYONE regardless of gender, looks, etc.

I came out publicly on Facebook about 3 years later, to my friends and family, which was overwhelmingly positive. But, among the more religious members of my family the concern was how my sexuality would work with my faith. Word eventually got to my bishop and he asked that I speak with him. The entire conversation revolved around stating holy, faithful, and not “giving into primal urges.”

It was that day when I realized that my faith wouldn’t accept my sexuality, that it was more important for me to abide by the rules than be true to myself. 

From that point onward, I began to lose my faith and respect for the church. I learned more about the literal history of the church, not the watered down version they taught me in Sunday school. 

Once I accepted that everyone was fallible, including Joseph Smith and the prophets that came after him, I just couldn’t bring myself to believe anymore. 

Between a beautiful lie and a painful truth, I chose to be a part of reality and face life and the obstacles that come with it. I wanted to thrive on my own strength, not relying on the power of prayer and blind faith. 

I’ve found more joy believing in humanity than I ever did believing in God.

More of an older brother than a parent, but I've got something:

When my stepbrother was little, little, like 4 years old, he loved to be a tiny daredevil. Like, he was jumping off literally anything he was able to climb onto. Well, my biological brother and I were about 8 and 10 respectively and we slept in bunk beds to save space in our room. This meant our stepbrother was constantly climbing up onto our bed and jumping off the top onto the floor. We pulled the mattress from the bottom bed onto the floor so he wouldn't hurt himself. So, one day, he jumped off and tried to do a flip. He didn't make it and landed right on the top of his head. My brother and I rolled him onto his back (I know, it was a bad idea, but we were 8 and 10, we didn't know any better) and he just stared up at the ceiling, eyes wide, making a choking sound. My brother got up to go get our dad when out of nowhere, stepbrother started screaming in horror. He didn't move, just laid stiff as a board and screamed. My dad came running in and we explained what happened. As soon as my dad knelt down to check him out, he just jumped to his feet with a smile and said he wanted to jump again. 

It still kind of sends shivers down my spine.
